title: Comments, Documentation, and When Not to Comment
learningObjectives: Distinguish helpful comments from comments that restate code.
Explain when documentation should describe intent or constraints.
Write comments that remain accurate as code changes.
Choose between inline comments, documentation, and clearer code.

understand.concept: Comments and documentation support understanding when they explain intent, constraints, decisions, assumptions, or non-obvious behavior. A comment that simply restates a clear line adds noise. Comments can become incorrect when code changes, so they are part of maintenance and must be reviewed. Documentation has different audiences and scope: a brief inline note helps near a decision, while README or API documentation explains usage and contracts. When code can be made self-explanatory through names or structure, prefer that over a redundant comment.
understand.whyItMatters: Readable, consistent code is easier to review, debug, and safely modify. These habits reduce unnecessary mental effort without replacing testing or design.
understand.analogy: Think of source code as instructions shared with a future teammate: clear labels and organization help them follow the route.
understand.analogyLimit: Analogies simplify collaboration; code still has precise rules, scope, and runtime behavior.

explain.narrative: A useful comment answers a question the code itself cannot easily answer: why a constraint exists, why an unusual approach was chosen, or what callers must guarantee. Avoid narrating every statement. Document public interfaces, important assumptions, and setup steps. If a comment and code disagree, readers may trust the wrong one—remove or update the comment immediately.

examples.title: Comment the reason for a constraint
examples.code: // Keep the final slot for a summary row.\nconst visibleRows = rows.slice(0, -1);\nconsole.log(visibleRows.length);
examples.explanation: The comment explains a design reason, not syntax.

examples.title: Avoid restating code
examples.explanation: A comment like 'set retryLimit to 3' would add no insight.

examples.title: Document a precondition
examples.explanation: The function makes an invalid condition explicit; documentation can clarify caller expectations.

examples.title: Mark a non-obvious trade-off
examples.explanation: A concise comment preserves the reason for a choice.

examples.title: Keep docs aligned with behavior
examples.explanation: When behavior changes, update its description and examples together.

commonMistakes: Using short or vague names that hide intent.
Applying personal style inconsistently with the project.
Treating formatting or comments as proof of correctness.
Making broad cosmetic changes mixed with logic edits.
Leaving comments or documentation stale after behavior changes.

guidedTask.title: Guided Practice
guidedTask.instructions: Inspect a snippet with three redundant comments and one unexplained assumption. Remove comments that merely repeat code. Add one concise note explaining the assumption or trade-off. Check whether names or structure could replace a comment. Review the final comments for accuracy and audience.

independentTask.title: Independent Practice
independentTask.instructions: Write a small function with a public contract and one non-obvious decision. Add documentation describing inputs, output, and constraints. Include only comments that add context beyond the code. Create a redundant comment, then remove it and explain why. Recheck all notes after a small code change.

options: Usage, contract, inputs, outputs, and constraints
questions.answer: Usage, contract, inputs, outputs, and constraints

questions.prompt: If code can be made clear through a descriptive name, what is often preferable?
options: Improve the code instead of adding a redundant comment
Copy a comment from another function
questions.answer: Improve the code instead of adding a redundant comment
questions.explanation: Self-explanatory code reduces the need for narration.
